title: The Seeker's Question
on_slide_text: Old sage Valmiki lives in a forest hut and knows every holy book. Yet one question troubles him. He asks the travelling sage Narada: who in this world is good in every way — loved by people and feared by demons in battle?
rationale: Opens on Valmiki's hook question to Narada, establishing the criterion quest that frames the entire Ramayana.

title: Measure Before Hero
question: Why does Valmiki ask Narada who the complete man is at this time before beginning the tale, instead of simply starting Rama's story?
answer: Valmiki first writes down what makes a person great — thankfulness, truth, strong promises, and love for people. Without such a measure, a story is only fun, not a guide. And Narada's yes proves that such a perfect person can really live — so write your three rules of life, and test every hero you admire by them.
on_slide_text: Why build a measure before telling a hero's story? Because without thankfulness and truth as your scale, a story stays only fun. Valmiki first writes what makes a person great — then finds the man. Write your three rules of life, and test every hero by them.
rationale: Pauses right after the hook to unpack why method precedes story, drawn from the first reflection.

title: Rama Named
on_slide_text: Narada smiles with joy and answers: Rama, prince of Ayodhya. He is calm, truthful, patient, and kind. As Narada speaks, Rama himself appears in a golden vision, bow in hand, ready to save the world.
rationale: Delivers Narada's delighted answer naming Rama, the central beat that the ideal exists.

title: Body Certifies Soul
on_slide_text: What does a perfect hero look like? Broad shoulders to carry duty, a calm face, eyes that see everyone equally. Rama stands before his shining city, and beside him glow the wheel of duty and the book of wise laws.
rationale: Presents the full portrait beat where physical marks and cosmic similes together certify moral stature.

title: Flesh Shows Virtue
question: Why does Narada string bodily marks like a conch-like neck and knee-long arms in the same garland as moral virtues like truth, forgiveness and compassion?
answer: This is not worship of the body. The body is like a report card of the heart — a broad chest means readiness to carry duty, big eyes mean seeing everyone as equal, a calm cool face means victory over anger. Goodness lives in our daily body. So once a day, without a mirror, notice your shoulders, your breath, your eyes — and ask what goodness they are showing.
on_slide_text: Why join body with virtue? Because the body is the heart's report card — a broad chest carries duty, big eyes see all as equal, a calm face beats anger. Once a day, without a mirror, notice your shoulders, breath and eyes, and ask what goodness they show.
rationale: Reflects on the portrait just shown, explaining why flesh and virtue belong in one garland.

title: Two Boons Exile
on_slide_text: King Dasharatha is ready to crown his eldest son Rama. Then Rama's stepmother Kaikeyi stops the joy. She claims two old promises: her own son Bharata must be king, and Rama must spend fourteen years in the forest.
rationale: Covers the turning beat where coronation hope flips to exile by boons and duty.

title: Ganga to Chitrakuta
on_slide_text: Rama accepts exile with a calm heart. His wife Sita and brother Lakshmana walk beside him into the forest. At the river, the boatman Guha ferries them across, while the royal chariot waits to carry the sad news home.
rationale: Follows the forest departure beat with Lakshmana, Sita, Guha and farewell to Ayodhya.

title: Sandals of Trust
on_slide_text: Bharata loves Rama and refuses the stolen throne. He begs Rama to return, but Rama keeps his father's word. So Bharata carries Rama's sandals to Nandigrama and rules the kingdom in his brother's name.
rationale: Completes the Ayodhya aftermath with death, refusal, sandals and waiting rule at Nandigrama.

title: Power as Trust
question: Why does Rama accept an unjust exile to protect Dasharatha's word, and why does Bharata, offered an unsought kingdom, leave with the sandals for Nandigrama?
answer: The real issue is trust, not orders. If the king's promise broke, no one's promise would be safe — so Rama gives up his right to keep everyone's faith alive. And Bharata refuses a throne won by trickery, so that order does not break twice. For both, power is a trust, not a prize. So before taking any gift you did not earn, wait a day and ask: will it grow trust?
on_slide_text: Why does Rama accept exile while Bharata refuses a free throne? Because the real issue is trust, not orders. Rama keeps the king's word so all promises stay safe; Bharata refuses a tricked throne so order never breaks. Power is a trust, not a prize.
rationale: Interprets the exile and sandals beats as a shared psychology of trust over power.

title: Vow Against Rakshasas
on_slide_text: Deep in Dandaka forest, holy sages beg Rama for safety from demons. The great sage Agastya blesses him, gives him god-made weapons, and Rama promises: your prayers will be protected.
rationale: Marks entry into Dandaka, arming by Agastya and the vow that launches the forest war.

title: Fourteen Thousand Fall
on_slide_text: Shurpanakha runs crying to the demon chief Khara, and his fourteen thousand soldiers rush at Rama. Alone and calm, lotus-eyed Rama lifts his great bow and faces them all by himself.
rationale: Isolates the Janasthana battle beat where disfigurement triggers mass slaughter.

title: The Luring
on_slide_text: A golden deer lures Rama and Lakshmana far from home. All is quiet in the empty hut. Then Sita hears a cry for help from the trees — and takes a step toward the sound.
rationale: Isolates the luring beat: empty seats, footprints, Sita alone hearing the cry, Maricha offstage.

title: Abduction Grief
on_slide_text: Demon king Ravana swoops down and carries Sita away into the sky. Only the brave old vulture Jatayu dares to stop him, diving with wide wings to bar the demon's path.
rationale: Preserves the climactic abduction beat with Maricha's warning, illusion, Jatayu and grief unmerged.

title: Grief
on_slide_text: Rama returns to find feathers strewn and the courtyard empty. His bow lies forgotten on the ground. Kneeling by the cold fire, Rama weeps for his stolen Sita.
rationale: Holds Rama's grief at the emptied hermitage before the funeral rites.

title: Rites
on_slide_text: With love and honour, Rama and Lakshmana burn brave Jatayu on a bed of flowers under the stars. Then the two brothers turn south, where new friends and new dangers wait.
rationale: Gives Jatayu's rites their own beat before the southern turn; Kabandha and Shabari stay in narration.

title: Shabari to Friendship
on_slide_text: On Pampa's bank the two brothers meet Hanuman, and he brings them to Sugriva. Before a witness fire, Rama and Sugriva join hands in lifelong friendship.
rationale: Traces the search chain from funeral rites through Kabandha and Shabari to Hanuman and alliance.

title: Proof
on_slide_text: Monkey king Sugriva doubts Rama's strength. So Rama smiles, hurls the demon's old bones far away, and with one arrow pierces seven tall palm trees. Doubt washed away!
rationale: Shows the strength-tests that cure Sugriva's doubt before the duel; bones are props.

title: Fall of Vali
on_slide_text: Sugriva roars his challenge at the gates of Kishkindha. His brother Vali storms out, strong as a mountain. Then Rama's single arrow flies from the trees — and unjust Vali falls.
rationale: Shows proof of strength and the single-arrow fall of Vali that wins Sugriva's kingdom.

title: Periphery Saves Center
question: Why must Ayodhya's prince make a fire-witnessed friendship with forest-dwellers like Sugriva and Hanuman to win over Ravana?
answer: When the center breaks, the edges save. Palace tricks took Rama's kingdom away, but the forest gave him searchers, an army, and wings — Hanuman's hundred-leap journey to the Ashoka garden shows that great tales are won by friendships, not by strength alone. The hero wins by joining a new world. So whenever you are stuck, ask one person outside your rank and circle for help.
on_slide_text: Why must a prince befriend forest monkeys? Because when the center breaks, the edges save. Exile took Rama's palace but gave him searchers, an army, and wings — great tales are won by friendship, not strength. Stuck? Ask help outside your rank.
rationale: Reflects on the forest alliance just formed, framing it as the epic's modern signal.

title: Leap to Ashoka
on_slide_text: Hanuman leaps across the whole sea in one mighty jump. In Lanka's Ashoka garden he finds Sita, sad but brave. He gives her Rama's ring and promises: Rama will come like a storm for you.
rationale: Covers the search climax with leap, discovery, token, comfort and capture.

title: Burning
on_slide_text: Caught, then freed by a gods-given blessing, Hanuman forgives his captors. He spares only Sita's garden, sets all Lanka on fire with his burning tail, and leaps away into the night.
rationale: Stages the merciful burning with no victims shown; captors stay faceless and off-frame.

title: Lanka Burns Ocean Rises
on_slide_text: Hanuman brings happy news: Sita is found! But the wide sea blocks the way. Rama draws his bow at the waves until Ocean himself rises, holding gifts, and shows them how to cross.
rationale: Links burning of Lanka and glad news to troubling the ocean, bridging search to invasion.

title: Bridge
on_slide_text: Stone by stone, the monkey army builds a floating bridge across the sea. Rama walks first on the new road, Hanuman lifts the heaviest boulders, and behind them the army marches stone by stone.
rationale: Shows the living bridge with Nala offstage and the vanara host as a faceless mass.

title: Bridge Battle Fire
on_slide_text: Saved, yet doubted — poor Sita must prove her truth. She walks calmly into roaring fire, and wonder! The flames curl around her like cool flowers. Fire-god Agni himself appears and declares her pure.
rationale: Holds the central climax unmerged away: bridge, killing, fire ordeal and new throne.

title: Return and Golden Rule
on_slide_text: The gods bless Rama, the fallen wake up, and all hurry home — Rama sends Hanuman flying ahead to tell Bharata: we are coming!
rationale: Closes the story arc with revival, Pushpaka return, coronation and Ramarajya merit.

title: Coronation
on_slide_text: At Nandigrama, Bharata returns the sandals' trust and offers Rama the crown with both hands. Crowned king of Ayodhya with Sita smiling beside him, Rama watches all the people dance with joy.
rationale: Crowns the return at Ayodhya with the family whole; crowd stays a rejoicing mass.

title: Love Tested Order Promised
question: Why does Rama speak harsh words before all after winning Sita back, and why does the tale then imagine a Ramarajya with no untimely death or fear?
answer: This is the double test of the ideal. Public doubt hurts even private love — Rama pays the price of becoming a man of limits, while Sita, walking into fire, declares she is her own. The Ramarajya that follows is not a report but a promise: a land with no fear, no hunger, no theft. Even the ideal can err, so we need an ideal order. Choose proof and talk before blame — and make one firm rule for fearlessness.
on_slide_text: Why harsh words after victory? Because public doubt wounds even private love. Rama pays the price of limits; Sita, walking into fire, declares she is her own. So ask for proof before blame — and build one fearless rule at home.
rationale: Ends on the sharpest insight, turning fire ordeal and Ramarajya vow into closing moral.
